prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker sits beside a gravely ill man in a cancer ward, surrounded by stark images of death, contamination, and medical machinery.
- While browsing a dating app and considering meeting another patient, the speaker instead chooses to stay and make the sick man laugh.
- The speaker admires the man’s altered appearance after chemotherapy while wishing his illness could be removed as simply as metal drawn out by a magnet.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A speaker confronting a loved one’s cancer uses stark, list-like hospital imagery, dark humor, digital encounters, and fantasies of healing and intimacy to document illness and helplessness. The poem finds that, although language cannot save the sick man, memory—especially his laugh—may preserve his vitality and offer refuge after loss.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: while he lives

outputs.L1:
While he lives, here’s a list of images: light in a filthy glass; a pigeon dead on the high, spiked window; a clear plastic bag above him, full of water—as if water could kill everything that lives in you, & it can.

I sit in a corner of the cancer ward, fingering the app that shows me other faggots in this hospital. I chat with one I might meet in radiology, but don’t. Instead, I make the sick man laugh while he’s conscious, compliment his gown, his new, brutal cheekbones that appeared with the chemo.

If only it were as simple as a magnet sucking the bad metals out of him. If only I could make a better list—more magic, less language; periphrastic & restorative. If only I had met that stranger in the basement & our pleasure had risen through the hospital, a bliss poultice for the sorrow-skinned who sit half-conscious & half-machinery.

While the sick man lives, all I can do is recount the vast pastoral of his illness. When he is gone, I’m counting on all the good flooding back: his beard, a collapsed country I’ll take refuge inside; his laugh, a memory so liquid I’ll hear it whenever anyone opens a window to scare the birds.
outputs.L2:
As long as he remains alive, I keep an inventory of what surrounds us: brightness dulled by a grimy pane; a pigeon’s body caught on the window’s tall metal spikes; a transparent bag suspended above him, filled with water—as though water might wash away every living thing inside a person, which it is capable of doing.

From a corner of the oncology ward, I scroll through an app that locates other gay men in the hospital. I message someone I could meet downstairs in radiology, though I never go. Instead, while the patient is awake, I try to coax laughter from him. I praise his hospital gown and the severe new angles of his face, carved out by chemotherapy.

I wish healing were no more difficult than drawing poisoned metal from his body with a magnet. I wish I could compose another kind of inventory—one with enchantment instead of words, indirect yet able to restore. I wish I had met the stranger in the basement, and that our pleasure had climbed through every floor of the hospital, becoming a joyful balm for those wrapped in grief, suspended between awareness and machines.

While the ill man is still here, my only act is to chronicle the immense landscape of his disease. After he dies, I trust that everything good will surge back: his beard, a ruined nation where I can seek shelter; his laughter, a memory fluid enough to be heard whenever someone raises a window and startles the birds away.
outputs.L3:
In a cancer ward marked by the stark presence of death, contamination, and medical machinery, the speaker sits beside a gravely ill man. The hospital environment makes the body’s vulnerability impossible to ignore: illness has transformed the patient, while the instruments meant to sustain him also emphasize the severity of his condition.

Although the speaker browses a dating app and briefly considers meeting another patient, they ultimately choose to remain at the man’s bedside. Rather than seeking distraction or connection elsewhere, the speaker devotes their attention to making him laugh. This small act becomes a gesture of tenderness and resistance, creating a moment of warmth within a place dominated by suffering.

The speaker also looks lovingly at the man’s appearance after chemotherapy, finding beauty in the ways treatment has changed him. At the same time, they wish his illness could be removed quickly and cleanly, like a piece of metal pulled from the body by a magnet. This impossible desire reveals both deep affection and helplessness: the speaker can offer companionship, but cannot extract the disease.

Throughout the scene, the speaker imagines language, intimacy, and pleasure as potential sources of healing. They long for words and human connection to do what medicine may no longer be able to accomplish—to soothe pain, restore dignity, and bring comfort to those suffering throughout the hospital.

Yet the man’s likely death remains unavoidable. In response, the speaker carefully records the landscape of his illness, preserving details of his altered body, his beard, and his laughter. These memories become a form of refuge: although they cannot prevent his death, they may allow the speaker to carry something of him forward after he is gone.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker struggling to confront a loved one’s cancer and the helplessness that accompanies it. Rather than describing illness in abstract or sentimental terms, the speaker records the experience through stark, list-like images of hospitals, medical procedures, and the body under pressure. This accumulation of clinical details suggests both shock and an attempt to impose order on an uncontrollable situation. By naming what can be seen, counted, or remembered, the speaker tries to make the illness manageable, even as the fragmented form reveals how difficult it is to understand emotionally.

Dark humor provides another way of enduring the crisis. Jokes do not diminish the seriousness of the cancer; instead, they interrupt the language of fear and medicine, briefly restoring the sick man’s personality. Digital encounters similarly complicate the experience of closeness. Screens and messages allow connection, but they also emphasize distance: the speaker can see or hear the loved one without being able to touch, comfort, or cure him. In response, the poem turns toward fantasies of healing and intimacy. These imagined scenes express the speaker’s desire to protect the man, restore his body, and escape the limits imposed by illness.

Ultimately, however, the poem recognizes that language cannot perform the miracle the speaker wants from it. Words can document suffering, express love, and resist emotional numbness, but they cannot save the sick man. The poem therefore shifts from rescue to preservation. Memory becomes a refuge after loss, keeping alive qualities that illness cannot fully erase. Most important is the memory of the man’s laugh, which embodies his humor, warmth, and vitality. By holding on to that sound, the speaker preserves something more intimate than a medical record: a sense of the person as he was beyond cancer. The poem cannot defeat death, but it can carry the loved one’s presence forward, transforming memory into a fragile form of survival.
outputs.L5:
While he lives, hope remains.

He may stumble, lose his way, or carry regrets too heavy to name, but each morning offers him another chance. While he lives, he can apologize, forgive, begin again, and become more than the mistakes behind him. The future is not promised, yet it is still open.

And while he lives in the memories of those who love him—in their stories, their laughter, and the lessons he left behind—a part of him will continue to endure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, stream-of-consciousness prose poem about a queer speaker visiting a dying man in a cancer ward, mixing grief, desire, dark humor, and surreal hospital imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
The elevator opens its metal mouth and says oncology like a curse it learned from a priest, and I step out carrying supermarket lilies wrapped in cellophane, already funeral-shaped, already sweating, while the nurses move under fluorescent moons with their rubber soles whispering hush hush hush though nobody here is sleeping, not really, not with the machines rehearsing their tiny electronic griefs.

You are in bed nine, thinner than the last lie you told me—*I’m fine, babe, don’t make it dramatic*—which is funny now because drama has made itself comfortable everywhere, has hung its sequined coat on the IV stand, has ordered room service, has shaved your beautiful head and left one silver hair on the pillow like a punchline too cruel even for us.

I say, You look hot.

You say, Necrophile.

Still flirting, then. Still us.

Your hand is a bird skeleton in mine and I remember it heavy on my thigh under the table at that terrible straight wedding, your thumb drawing circles through my trousers while somebody’s uncle explained marriage to us as if we had not already survived three landlords, two Pride riots, your mother’s Christmas, my fear of being touched in daylight. Desire is a stupid animal. It keeps licking the locked door. Even here, where your gown opens at the back and your chest is mapped with tape, I want to climb inside your warmth, what remains of it, want to kiss the morphine from your mouth, want the orderly to stop coming in every six minutes to ask whether you’ve passed urine.

Have you passed urine?

No, but I’ve passed judgment, you say.

The orderly does not laugh. Amateur.

Outside, a trolley rattles by carrying silver domes, each one hiding mashed potatoes or a small moon or somebody’s excised sorrow. The corridor lengthens whenever I look at it. The hand-sanitizer dispensers are pale plastic saints. The MRI downstairs dreams in magnets. Somewhere a tumor glows like a nightclub we were never invited to, cells dancing past last call, multiplying with the vulgar confidence of men who have never been told no.

I hate your cancer’s ambition.

I hate how everyone calls it a battle, as if you misplaced your sword, as if dying means you didn’t want life badly enough. You wanted it obscenely. You sucked marrow from it. You wore red leather to the courthouse. You kissed me once in a cathedral and said God can file a complaint.

Now God is apparently busy with paperwork.

I wet the sponge and touch it to your lips. This tenderness embarrasses me more than sex ever did. Your eyes open, green and furious, and for one second I see the old you—the you who stole hotel towels, who danced shirtless in winter, who called every dog “Madam”—and then the morphine lifts you gently by the collar and carries you somewhere I cannot follow.

I talk anyway. I tell you the lilies look vaginal, aggressively so. I tell you your ex sent love, though what he actually sent was a thumbs-up emoji, that tiny yellow bastard. I tell you I forgive you for leaving, then take it back because you haven’t left yet, then apologize because language keeps getting ahead of the body.

The monitor writes its green sentence over and over.

The monitor refuses punctuation.

Night presses its face to the window. In the glass I see us layered over the city: your bed floating above traffic, my queer little grief in its borrowed chair, towers blinking red like warning lights on a spaceship that has already hit the asteroid. I imagine the ward detaching from the hospital, rising whole into the dark—beds, pumps, lilies, nurses, all of us ascending past weather, past doctrine, past the bouncer at heaven who checks the guest list and says there’s been a mistake.

There has been a mistake.

There has been—

You squeeze my hand, or the muscles do, or I invent it. Love has always been partly invention. So has survival. So has God. I lean down until my forehead touches yours, careful of the tubes, careful of nothing, and you smell like antiseptic and salt and the last warm room in the world.

Don’t go, I think.

Go, I think.

I’m here, I say, which is the only spell I know, and the machines keep blinking their indifferent stars, and your mouth tilts almost into a smile, almost wicked, almost alive enough to ruin me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary queer poem about using a hookup app in a hospital while keeping vigil beside someone undergoing chemotherapy; contrast bodily pleasure with illness, machinery, memory, and impending loss.
counterfactuals.output:
**Nearby**

In the infusion ward, everyone is looking  
for a vein, a future, a place  
to put the needle.

Beside me, you sleep beneath a warmed blanket,  
your blood taking the long mechanical road  
out of the body, through clear chambers, back—  
a red sentence revised by machines.

My phone glows under the hospital sheet:

**900 feet away.**  
**Into kissing, sweat, no expectations.**  
A torso cropped clean of history.  
A mouth saying *now* without saying *after.*

I swipe as quietly as prayer.

Once, in a club bathroom, you held my hair  
while I vomited cheap gin and glitter.  
Once, you taught me the difference  
between loneliness and wanting to be touched.  
Now the pump keeps its bright arithmetic.  
Now your face has the soft, unfinished look  
of a photograph still loading.

A man messages: **you hosting?**

Above us, fluorescent tubes hum  
their sterile little heaven.  
The plastic bag empties  
one medicinal star at a time.

I type: **At the hospital. Complicated.**  
He sends a heart, then a question mark,  
then nothing.

My body, traitorous animal,  
still imagines his hands—  
how pleasure can make a door  
where there is only wall,  
how for several breathless minutes  
the flesh believes it is not mortal.

You wake and ask what time it is.

I tell you.  
I do not tell you the doctor said *months*,  
as if loss were a lease expiring,  
as if memory could pack us into boxes:  
your first wig, your old pronouns,  
the voicemail where you laugh so hard  
the microphone breaks into weather.

On the app, bodies orbit the building—  
nurses on break, sons of the dying,  
men whose names disappear by morning.  
Blue dots pulsing through concrete,  
each of us asking the dark  
if anyone is near enough  
to make us briefly undeniable.

I put the phone facedown.

The machine alarms.  
A nurse arrives, presses silence.

In that sudden hush, you reach for my hand—  
not romance, not rescue,  
just skin finding skin  
beside the cold, exact machinery.

Outside, someone is taking off his shirt.  
Outside, the city is all appetite.

Here, your fingers close around mine,  
and I let them—  
the living body warm,  
the losing body warm,  
no difference yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, fragmented hospital poem featuring a dead pigeon, a plastic bag of water, radiology, a patient’s brutal new cheekbones, and the impossible wish to draw sickness from the body like metal with a magnet.
counterfactuals.output:
**Radiology**

Outside the automatic doors,  
a dead pigeon  
keeps one blue-gray wing  
open to weather—

as if flight were interrupted  
by a question  
no one could answer.

Inside, fluorescent noon.  
A plastic bag of water  
hangs from its silver tree,  
clear as an unfinished prayer,

dripping its small, measured mercy  
into the arm.

Radiology—  
the dark room’s mechanical stars,  
the body translated  
into weather maps:

cloud in the lung,  
white road of bone,  
a shadow flowering  
where no flower should.

The patient turns.

Illness has carved  
brutal new cheekbones  
beneath the skin—  
two blades, two cold moons—

and still the nurse says  
hold still,  
as though stillness could save us.

I want a magnet  
large as grief.

I want to pass it  
over the chest, the blood,  
the trembling abdomen—

draw sickness from the body  
like metal,

hear each hidden shard  
rise with a bright click,

lift free  
into the merciful air.

But the machine hums.  
The bag empties.  
Rain beads the glass.

Outside, the pigeon  
does not move,

except in the reflection  
of everyone leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a dense prose poem in lowercase with ampersands instead of “and,” minimal punctuation, visceral metaphors, and a speaker trying to preserve a sick loved one through lists, laughter, and memory.
counterfactuals.output: i inventory you against the dark  three blue pills  half a pear  the cracked cup sweating beside the bed  seven freckles at your wrist like seeds refusing burial  i write everything down because the body is a house already packing its boxes  because fever licks your bones clean  because your breath keeps snagging on the ribs like wet cloth on a fence  so i list the names you gave the neighborhood cats  the songs you ruined beautifully  the summer you laughed milk through your nose & we collapsed on the kitchen floor while the toast burned into black little doors  laugh again i say  let me hear that bright animal kick its cage  let me seal it in a jar with the birthday candles & bus tickets & every small mercy we forgot to call mercy  outside the rain thumbs the window  inside your blood drags its red suitcase down a narrowing hall  i press my ear to your chest & memorize the failing machinery  each stutter  each flooded spark  as if memory were salt  as if naming could cure meat of death  as if i could keep you by counting  one scar  two dimples  three times you forgave me  four winters asleep with your cold feet tucked beneath my knees  i count until numbers become teeth  until grief tastes iron  until morning opens its pale mouth & i am still feeding it your name
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
